title: Syllogisms
source: MindSpark Grade 8 Aptitude & Reasoning | Chapter 3: Syllogisms
subtopics: Statement types: All A are B, Some A are B, No A is B, Some A are not B
Venn diagram method for syllogism validation
learningGoals: Draw accurate Venn diagrams for each of the four syllogism statement types
Determine whether a conclusion definitely follows, possibly follows, or does not follow
Identify complementary pairs that together are always true
Avoid common traps: assuming converse, assuming contradiction
coreIdeas: All A are B → A circle is entirely inside B circle
Some A are B → A and B circles overlap partially
No A is B → A and B circles are completely separate
Some A are not B → part of A is outside B; A and B may partially overlap
A conclusion 'definitely follows' only when it is true in ALL possible Venn diagrams; 'possibly follows' if true in at least one

workedExamples.problem: Statements: All cats are animals. All animals are living things. Conclusion I: All cats are living things. Conclusion II: Some living things are cats. Do the conclusions follow?
workedExamples.solution: Cats ⊆ Animals ⊆ Living Things. Therefore Cats ⊆ Living Things — Conclusion I: Definitely follows. Since all cats are living things, some living things are cats — Conclusion II: Definitely follows. Both conclusions are valid.

workedExamples.problem: Statements: Some doctors are engineers. All engineers are rich. Conclusion I: Some doctors are rich. Conclusion II: All doctors are rich. Do the conclusions follow?
workedExamples.solution: Some doctors fall in the engineers circle. All engineers are inside rich. So those doctors who are engineers are also rich → Some doctors are rich. Conclusion I: Definitely follows. Not all doctors need to be engineers, so not all doctors are rich. Conclusion II: Does not follow.

workedExamples.problem: Statements: No birds are fish. Some fish are mammals. Conclusion I: No birds are mammals. Conclusion II: Some mammals are not birds. Do the conclusions follow?
workedExamples.solution: Birds and fish are disjoint. Some fish are in mammals. The fish-mammals overlap tells us nothing about birds-mammals overlap (they could touch or not). Conclusion I: Does not definitely follow (birds and mammals may or may not overlap). Conclusion II: Since some fish are mammals and no fish are birds, those fish-mammals are not birds — so some mammals (at least the fish-mammals) are not birds. Conclusion II: Definitely follows.

onboarding.coachIntro: Syllogisms are pure logic — no subject knowledge needed, just Venn diagram power. Once you master the 4 statement types, you'll answer every syllogism question with 100% confidence.
onboarding.placementRule: If learner selects 'I have done this before', skip Exercise A and start at Exercise C.

mission.missionPromise: You will correctly classify All, Some, No, and Some-Not statements and determine definite vs possible conclusions for any 2–3 statement syllogism.
mission.successCelebration: Logic Champion badge unlocked! You validated every conclusion with Venn diagram precision!

microLessonPattern: Draw the Venn diagram for each statement type

beats.teacherLine: Syllogisms use Venn diagrams as lie detectors. Each statement type draws a specific picture. 'All A are B' → circle A is fully inside circle B. 'Some A are B' → A and B overlap partially. 'No A is B' → circles are completely apart. Once you draw these, the conclusion either appears in the picture or it doesn't.
beats.boardAction: Draw three separate Venn diagrams side by side: (1) A fully inside B for 'All A are B', (2) A and B overlapping for 'Some A are B', (3) A and B separate for 'No A is B'. Label each clearly.
beats.checkpointPrompt: Which Venn diagram shows 'All dogs are mammals'?
beats.expectedStudentResponse: Dogs circle fully inside mammals circle
beats.fallbackHint: All dogs are mammals means every dog is also a mammal — so the dogs circle fits entirely inside the mammals circle.

beats.teacherLine: Watch me check a conclusion. Statements: Some doctors are engineers. All engineers are rich. I draw: partial overlap between Doctors and Engineers. Then Engineers circle sits fully inside Rich circle. Now I look at the picture — is any part of Doctors inside Rich? Yes! The overlapping engineers-doctors part is inside Rich. So 'Some doctors are rich' definitely follows.
beats.boardAction: Draw three circles: Doctors (left), Engineers (middle, overlapping with Doctors), Rich (Engineers circle sits inside Rich). Shade the Doctors-Engineers overlap region and show it is inside Rich.
beats.checkpointPrompt: From the same statements, does 'All doctors are rich' follow?
beats.fallbackHint: Look at the Venn diagram — part of the Doctors circle is outside the Engineers circle and therefore outside Rich. Not all doctors need to be rich.

beats.teacherLine: Your turn. Statements: No birds are fish. Some fish are mammals. Draw the diagram — Birds and Fish are separate circles. Fish and Mammals overlap. Look at this picture and decide: does 'No birds are mammals' definitely follow?
beats.boardAction: Draw: Birds circle (left, isolated). Fish circle (center). Mammals circle (right, overlapping with Fish). Show birds and mammals could or could not overlap.
beats.checkpointPrompt: Does 'No birds are mammals' definitely follow from 'No birds are fish' + 'Some fish are mammals'?
beats.expectedStudentResponse: No, it does not definitely follow
beats.fallbackHint: The Venn diagram doesn't tell us anything about the birds-mammals relationship. They could overlap or not — so we cannot say 'definitely'.

sessionFlow.coachHook: Before solving anything, draw the Venn diagram. The picture IS the answer.

boardDemo.title: 4 statement types — 4 diagrams
steps: All A are B → A inside B
Some A are B → partial overlap
No A is B → separated circles
Some A are not B → partial overlap, but part of A outside B
boardDemo.teacherLine: Memorise these 4 diagrams. Every syllogism is just one of these four pictures.

sessionFlow.readAloudPrompt: Draw all four diagrams on paper before continuing.
sessionFlow.tryPrompt: Which diagram matches: 'Some politicians are honest'?
sessionFlow.masteryCheck: Partial overlap between politicians and honest circles
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackWin: Correct! 'Some' always means partial overlap — a non-empty intersection.
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackRetry: Here's a trick: 'Some' = at least one is in both sets → draw two circles that share a region.
sessionFlow.reviewPrompt: How is 'Some A are not B' different from 'No A is B' in Venn diagrams?

sessionFlow.coachHook: All-All chains are the easiest — the conclusion is transitive. Let's verify it with Venn.

boardDemo.title: All-All transitive syllogism
steps: All A are B → A ⊆ B
All B are C → B ⊆ C
Therefore A ⊆ B ⊆ C → All A are C
Also: Some C are A (because A is inside C, A is non-empty)
boardDemo.teacherLine: In All-All chains, you always get a definite All conclusion going forward and a definite Some conclusion going backward.

sessionFlow.readAloudPrompt: Recite: 'All A in B, All B in C → All A in C.'
sessionFlow.tryPrompt: All roses are flowers. All flowers are plants. Does 'Some plants are roses' definitely follow?
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackWin: Exactly right! Roses ⊆ Flowers ⊆ Plants. Roses are inside Plants, so some plants (the roses) are roses.
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackRetry: Here's a trick: Roses are a subset of Plants (via the chain). So at least those roses are plants, meaning some plants are roses.
sessionFlow.reviewPrompt: In an All-All chain with A→B→C, which two conclusions definitely follow?

sessionFlow.coachHook: The golden rule: Some + All = Some (definite). Engrave this in your memory.

boardDemo.title: Some-All syllogism
steps: Some A are B → A and B overlap
All B are C → B ⊆ C
The A-B overlap is inside C → Some A are C (definite)
Cannot conclude All A are C
boardDemo.teacherLine: The overlap region between A and B gets 'carried' into C because all of B is inside C.

sessionFlow.readAloudPrompt: Say: 'Some A overlap B. All B inside C. The overlap lands in C.'
sessionFlow.tryPrompt: Some students are athletes. All athletes are disciplined. Which conclusion definitely follows: (a) All students are disciplined, (b) Some students are disciplined, (c) No students are disciplined?
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackWin: Correct! The athlete-students are definitely disciplined (since all athletes are disciplined). So some students (the athlete ones) are disciplined.
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackRetry: Here's a trick: Some students are athletes (overlap). All athletes are disciplined (athletes ⊆ disciplined). That overlap lands inside disciplined. → Some students are disciplined.
sessionFlow.reviewPrompt: Why can't we conclude 'All students are disciplined' from 'Some students are athletes'?

sessionFlow.missionStepTitle: Exercise D: The Power of No
sessionFlow.coachHook: 'No' statements are absolute. They give strong conclusions — and strong traps.

boardDemo.title: No-statement syllogism rules
steps: No A is B → A and B are completely separate
All A are B (contradicts No A is B if combined carelessly)
No A is B + All C are B → No A is C? Only if all of C is inside B and A is outside B
No A is B → Some B are not A (definitely)
boardDemo.teacherLine: When you see 'No A is B', immediately draw them as separated circles. Then check whether the conclusion requires them to touch — if yes, it does not follow.

sessionFlow.readAloudPrompt: Draw: No A is B → two circles with a clear gap between them.
sessionFlow.tryPrompt: No cats are dogs. All dogs are animals. Conclusion: No cats are animals. Does this follow?
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackWin: Exactly! Cats and dogs are separate. Dogs are inside animals. But cats could also be inside animals independently — we simply don't know. So 'No cats are animals' does not definitely follow.
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackRetry: Here's a trick: No cats=dogs and All dogs⊆animals doesn't say anything about cats vs animals. Cats could overlap with animals through a different path.
sessionFlow.reviewPrompt: From 'No A is B', what single conclusion ALWAYS definitely follows?

sessionFlow.coachHook: Exam questions love the word 'possibly'. A conclusion possibly follows if it's true in at least one valid diagram.

boardDemo.title: Possible conclusions and complementary pairs
steps: A conclusion 'possibly follows' = true in at least one Venn diagram arrangement
Complementary pair: one says 'Some A are B', other says 'No A is B' — exactly one must be true
If conclusion I doesn't definitely follow and conclusion II doesn't definitely follow, check if they are complementary
If complementary, the answer is 'Either I or II follows'
boardDemo.teacherLine: Complementary pairs are the trick answer option in competitive exams. Spot them by looking for one positive and one negative conclusion about the same pair.

sessionFlow.readAloudPrompt: Read: 'Complementary pairs: one must be true, the other false — but we don't know which.'
sessionFlow.tryPrompt: Statements: Some A are B. No B is C. Conclusion I: Some A are not C. Conclusion II: No A is C. Which follows?
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackWin: Correct! Some A are B. Those A that are B — are they C? No B is C, so those A (who are B) are not C. Therefore some A (the B ones) are not C. Conclusion I definitely follows.
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackRetry: Here's a trick: Some A are B → pick one such A. That A is also B. No B is C → that A is not C. So at least one A is not C → Some A are not C.
sessionFlow.reviewPrompt: Define a complementary pair of conclusions in the context of syllogisms.

sessionFlow.coachHook: Three premises, one conclusion. The chain must hold at every link.

boardDemo.title: 3-statement syllogism
steps: Apply statement 1 and 2 to get an intermediate conclusion
Apply the intermediate conclusion with statement 3
Draw a combined Venn with 3 or 4 circles
Read the final conclusion from the diagram
boardDemo.teacherLine: Three-statement chains are just two-statement syllogisms applied twice. Solve left to right.

sessionFlow.readAloudPrompt: Solve in two steps: (St1 + St2) → intermediate → (intermediate + St3) → final.
sessionFlow.tryPrompt: All A are B. All B are C. Some C are D. Which conclusion definitely follows: (a) All A are D, (b) Some A are D, (c) All A are C, (d) Some D are B?
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackWin: Spot on! All A→B→C, so All A are C (definite). Some C are D does NOT extend to all A. (a) doesn't follow. (b) doesn't definitly follow. (d) — some D are C; some C are B (reversing All B⊆C gives Some C are B). (d) is valid too but the most direct answer in this context is (c).
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackRetry: Here's a trick: All A⊆B, All B⊆C → All A⊆C. That's conclusion (c). Some C are D doesn't tell us which C — could be C that are not A.
sessionFlow.reviewPrompt: In a 3-statement All-All-Some chain (A→B→C, some C are D), does 'Some A are D' definitely follow?

sessionFlow.coachHook: Exam setters love three traps: converse error, conversion error, and complement confusion. Let's destroy all three.

boardDemo.title: Three syllogism traps
steps: Converse error: All A are B → wrongly concluding All B are A
Conversion: All A are B → correctly gives Some B are A (valid)
Complement confusion: Some A are not B ≠ No A is B
Trap: 'It is possible that no A is B' when Some A are B is given — impossible!
boardDemo.teacherLine: The converse of 'All' is 'Some', never 'All'. Burn this rule into your memory.

sessionFlow.readAloudPrompt: Recite: 'All A are B does NOT mean All B are A. It means Some B are A.'
sessionFlow.tryPrompt: All teachers are graduates. Conclusion: All graduates are teachers. Is this conclusion valid?
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackWin: Well spotted! 'All teachers are graduates' only tells us teachers ⊆ graduates. There are many graduates who are not teachers.
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackRetry: Here's a trick: Draw teachers circle inside graduates circle. The conclusion 'All graduates are teachers' would require graduates to be inside teachers — the reverse, which is NOT shown.
sessionFlow.reviewPrompt: What valid conclusion CAN be drawn from 'All A are B'? (Hint: involves 'Some')

sessionFlow.missionStepTitle: Exercise H: Olympiad Boss — Full Syllogism
sessionFlow.coachHook: Three statements. Four conclusions. Find all that follow. This is the format of every competitive exam.

boardDemo.title: Full syllogism evaluation
steps: Draw the combined Venn for all 3 statements
Test each conclusion independently
For inconclusive ones, check if they form a complementary pair
Report: Definitely follows / Possibly follows / Does not follow
boardDemo.teacherLine: Evaluate every conclusion separately — don't let an earlier conclusion influence your judgment of a later one.

sessionFlow.readAloudPrompt: Challenge: evaluate all four conclusions systematically.
sessionFlow.tryPrompt: Statements: Some pens are books. All books are papers. No paper is a pencil. Conclusions: I. Some pens are papers. II. No book is a pencil. III. Some papers are pens. IV. All pencils are books. Which conclusions definitely follow?
sessionFlow.masteryCheck: I, II, and III definitely follow
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackWin: Outstanding logic! I: Some pens are books, All books are papers → Some pens are papers ✓. II: All books are papers, No paper is a pencil → No book is a pencil ✓. III: Some pens are papers → Some papers are pens (valid conversion of 'some') ✓. IV: No paper is a pencil → pencils are outside papers → pencils outside books (since books ⊆ papers) → All pencils are books is FALSE ✗.
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackRetry: Here's a trick: Test I (Some-All chain), II (All-No chain = No conclusion), III (conversion of Some), IV (No + All relationship — check if pencils relate to books at all).
sessionFlow.reviewPrompt: What is the valid conversion of the statement 'Some A are B'?
